thread.title: Apple's And Microsoft's Cash: A Year Later - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Pinxter Analytics
title: Apple's And Microsoft's Cash: A Year Later - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Just over a year ago, on January 10th, 2018, I wrote an article titled Apple's And Microsoft's Shareholder Repatriation Is Not A Sure Thing , ( AAPL ) ( MSFT ) arguing that given the profit-above-all-else motive of corporations these days, they're likely to use the new tax law as a publicity stunt but not actually return most of the cash, and use elaborate ways to reduce their tax bills from the repatriation holiday (deemed repatriation, where all assets are deemed returned and taxed at a rate of 15.5% for liquid-assets and 8% for non-liquid assets).
Since, it's been clear that most corporations, with exceptions like Gilead Sciences ( GILD ) and Cisco Systems ( CSCO ), opted to leave most their cash overseas and spread the tax payments across 8 years as allowed in the new law. Based on the Federal Reserve report (linked in the article above), an estimated $465 billion has been repatriated throughout H1 of 2018, about one-sixth the amount of cash which is estimated to be held overseas. According to the Wall Street Journal report, which went through corporate filings and talked to management of 108 public companies with the largest amounts of cash held overseas, only $143 billion were brought back in to the country thus far with around $37 billion more intended to be brought back through the remainder of the fiscal year.
Even more so, mega companies like General Electric ( GE ) and Boston Scientific ( BSX ), according to the same Wall Street Journal research, said they have no need or intention to bring back the cash as they have non-liquid asset commitments overseas and will use the money for acquisitions and other activities.
My Prediction: What Actually Will Happen Prior to the actual law being passed and subsequent to it, a lot of numbers floated around without much regard to what the actual law entails. Most headlines were citing a single number - 15.5% on all the estimated $4 trillion held in cash overseas, no questions asked.
This wasn't true. For one thing, taxes already paid by a corporation on the aforementioned cash held (retained earnings) is considered paid and will not be subject to an additional tax, as stated in the tax code:
Subject to certain limitations, U.S. citizens, resident individuals, and domestic corporations are allowed to claim credit for foreign income taxes they pay. A domestic corporation that owns at least 10 percent of the voting stock of a foreign corporation is allowed a "deemed-paid" credit for foreign income taxes paid by the foreign corporation that the domestic corporation is deemed to have paid when the related income is distributed as a dividend or is included in the domestic corporation's income under the anti-deferral rules.
''If a domestic corporation chooses to have the benefits of subpart A of part III of subchapter N (redacted) for any taxable year, an amount equal to the taxes deemed to be paid by such corporation under subsections (A), (B) and (D) of section 960 (determined without regard to the phrase '80 percent of' in subsection) for such taxable year shall be treated for purposes of this title as a dividend received by such domestic corporation from the foreign corporation.''
The second point being that there were several more tax provisions, like the 8% on non-liquid assets and the fact that all companies had 8 years to pay their taxes on these assets so the actual tax bills were substantially lower than most estimates. Apple is likely not going to pay $38 billion and Microsoft will likely not pay $15 billion, since they've already paid taxes in Ireland and in Singapore on portions of those retained earnings (cash), even as some of it is being held in offshore accounts being taxed at a rate of 0.005% and will be subject to the full scope of the new taxing system.
So What Actually Happened? Apple stopped reporting cash information, but its other numbers show the full picture. First of all, its deferred income tax benefits jumped from $6 billion to $34.7 billion after the tax law came into effect meaning that the initial number of $38 billion tax bill was exaggerated. Second, their marketable securities have barely changed, meaning they have no intention on divesting and bringing back the cash, which is being invested from an overseas investment fund. The company's marketable securities (long and short term) were $248 billion in Q1, $222 billion in Q2, $212 billion in Q3 and $211 billion in Q4, indicating they did use the money from those sales for a massive stock repurchase push throughout the year. (All numbers are for fiscal 2018).
The company did hire 7,000 new employees in 2017 and 9,000 more in 2018 but the effects of higher income were not showing, as stock-based compensation rose from $4.2 billion to $4.8 billion in 2017 and again to $5.3 billion in 2018. Not only is this in line with what the company initially predicted it would do years before the tax cut was in place, it opted into income tax benefit boosting stock-based compensation which is limited to 85% of the employee's paycheck, which generated an additional $1.6 billion in income tax benefits for the company and didn't give much cash to employees.
Microsoft did not, as of late, seem to repatriate or restate any of the cash. Their cash pile remained at the same level it did before the enactment of the tax cuts at around $134 billion and their repatriation income taxes were pushed into deferred income taxes as they continue to figure out what they owe the US. Their tax bill did increase by $5 billion this year (deferred figure), meaning they will too spread the estimated $13.6 billion they owe in taxes on their cash stockpile over the course of a few years. The company did not announce any major changes to its cash distribution and will likely keep most of it outside the US as they look to invest in different areas around the globe.
The company hired an additional ~3,000 so far this year, based on external estimates, but had a neutral net hiring (excluding LinkedIn) in 2018 as employees rose from 124,000 to 131,000. The company did increase their stock-based compensation for employees, subject to almost identical bargaining agreements as Apple's, and enjoyed a healthy tax benefit for 2018. The company did not announce definitive plans to hire more employees in the United States but are working on active expansion in India and other Asia-Pacific region countries as the US market begins to saturate.
The Bigger Picture According to research done based off the numbers the Federal Reserve released about repatriated cash ($465 billion in H1 of 2018), it is estimated that $55 billion were spent on share repurchasing, and based on a Goldman Sachs report, companies will spend over $1 trillion on share buybacks this year alone.
As seen in jobs reports and headcount tallies from the largest US companies with large cash piles, an across-the-board pay raise or new hirings did not take place. Instead, one time bonuses, some restricted stock options and previously-planned hirings have taken place, boosting a quarter or two of consumer spending numbers but all-in-all making little difference for the workers of those companies but making a big difference to shareholders.
It is noteworthy to mention that the increase in dividends and buyback created a situation where stock prices surged in a very short period of time, followed by a rather large wave of selling, creating an incentive for investors to sell stocks within the one-year period required to take advantage of the capital gains tax. This will create some bump in income tax revenues for 2018 (filed in April of 2019) as regular tax rates apply when joined with annual income of dividends and do not qualify for the lower capital gains tax of 20%.
Moving Forward Apple is yet to announce a dividend hike for 2019 but its buyback activity is very visible this year. In the first 3 quarters of 2017, the company bought back $25.5 billion worth of stock, which grew 'slightly' by 147% to $63 billion for the same time period this year. It's clear that market dynamics had a lot more to do with this given their share price dipped from $222.00 per share at its peak to $155.00 per share as of late, but this trend is clearly a beneficiary of the recent tax overhaul alongside their new 2018 $100 billion repurchase authority. Remember, the fewer shares the company has the less they pay out in dividend so a large increase in dividend per share does not mean they're spending more money on shareholders.
It seems for now that the company is focusing on shareholder value and even divesting from future applications like some IoT ventures and automated vehicles and refocusing their attention in penetrating the Asia-Pacific markets with their existing, expensive technologies. This is by no means bad for shareholders, which may see their fortunes double throughout the next 2-3 years as buybacks and dividend payments increase, but there's a real worry beyond that point as to what the company will actually use its mountains of cash (beyond paying down debt) and how it will affect their long term future.
Microsoft did report a somewhat surprising bump in their quarterly dividend, hiking it from an expected $0.42 per share to $0.46 per share, even after they hiked dividend by a lower rate last year (+7.7%, down from +8.3% in 2017). It's still unclear how they intend to use their cash, besides funding acquisitions like LinkedIn or others in the works, but their buyback story is somewhat similar with a 94% Y/Y increase, even as it pales in comparison to other technology companies. Microsoft spent just over $3 billion in the first 3 quarters of the year compared to $1.6 billion it did in the year prior.
Moving forward, I believe Microsoft will use its cash pile and whatever it brings back to the US more wisely than Apple given their tendency for innovation over shareholder returns. This can be in the form of some larger acquisitions like the LinkedIn one (although I'm not at liberty to speculate) and boosting their overall R&D budgets as they prepare to enter the Internet of Things (IoT) and other future technologies in full scale in the near future.
Conclusion: Shareholders vs. The Future When it comes to investing in workers (if that were possible), it would be a bad investment. It doesn't seem that either company is using their tax holiday to invest in their workers and give them pay raises as we continue to see a large portion of overall wage increase numbers among certain industries and pay grades. (Hint: It's not the lower income folks).
If we were investing in a company based on pure numbers, Apple will still be my first choice for the shorter-term (1 to 2 years), given their commitment to return almost $1 trillion in buybacks and dividends to shareholders, potentially doubling your value in the aforementioned period of time. Another factor in mind is their current valuation and share price given pressures from China and the broad market selloff. The discussion on the future of Apple beyond the iPhone is the subject of an article I'll release in March (and the subject of a few dozen articles released thus far on Seeking Alpha), but until then you can read up on my thoughts in my previous articles Apple: You've Got This All Wrong about the Internet of Things and Apple: A New Growth Avenue Emerges where I discuss the Home Pod and its future.
From a long term standpoint of investing in technology (5 years), it's hard to beat Microsoft's vision of where technology will be in the future. It's investing heavily in technologies like the Internet of Things and others and it's saving its earnings to move into those technologies rather than spending it all on buybacks or special dividends. Sure, there's a limit to how much cash you can infuse into R&D budgets and it'll be unreasonable for Apple or any company to spend $150 billion in R&D but there's something to be said about the focus of a company whereas Apple focuses on its existing technologies (and divests from automated vehicles and some IoT prospects) while Microsoft doubles down on them. I think owning Microsoft for your kids' portfolios is a better choice than owning Apple, for the time being.
To sum things up, reality hit up the headlines when it came to what actually happened with this 'historic tax reform bill' and the real effects of which we are beginning to feel as some consumer spending begins to slow. Nonetheless, there is real optimism amongst companies which are using this tax holiday to look into the future, like Microsoft, or for Apple as they look for shorter term gains as they revamp their older products and look for what to do next with their moolah. All in all, it was a good thing to do, but don't expect $4 trillion to be invested in the United States any time soon.
Disclosure: I am/we are long MSFT, SHORT AAPL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
Additional disclosure: AAPL short represents a swing trade from the recent market slowdown and is not reflective of my long term views of the company throughout the article.
